The biggest risk of AI layoffs might not be mass job losses.

It might be the disappearance of the career ladder.

Here’s what some business leaders believe:

• Dario Amodei warns that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs.

• Jensen Huang believes AI will create new job opportunities.

• Andy Jassy expects AI-driven efficiency to reduce parts of Amazon’s corporate workforce.

• Jamie Dimon believes some jobs will disappear while new ones emerge.

But Brian Chesky raises a different concern that deserves more attention.

What happens when AI takes over the work traditionally assigned to interns and junior employees?

Where will the next generation learn how a business actually operates?

Future managers, executives and CEOs don't develop judgment overnight.

They learn by handling small tasks, making mistakes, solving unexpected problems and gradually taking on greater responsibility.

This is why the conversation about AI layoffs needs to go beyond headcount.

The goal shouldn't be to preserve every traditional task.

It should be to preserve the learning that prepares people for greater responsibility.

AI may reduce the need for certain entry-level tasks. But companies still need a way to develop future leaders.

Otherwise, the layoffs that improve efficiency today could create a leadership gap tomorrow.

And if you're looking for a new job, here's something worth remembering.

Applying to more jobs isn't always the answer. Finding the right opportunities matters.

If remote work is your goal, don't limit your search to LinkedIn.

Here are 24 platforms worth exploring.

1. Remote job websites

I really enjoy automating things, I can’t lie.

What I enjoy most is the engineering underneath. I like getting two systems that were never meant to talk to each other to work together and building a job that runs every morning without anyone touching it. I also like working out why something broke at 3am and making sure it can't break that way again.

That's the part I'm best at and it's the part I want to spend more of my time on.

So two things:

Picture the demo. 

A law firm is test-driving an AI research assistant. Answers in seconds. Every authority linked. The partners are sold. 

Now picture the blind associate who will use it every day. A screen reader can read the answer aloud. It can’t navigate the panel holding the sources. The firm expects every lawyer to verify the AI’s output — and has just chosen a tool that makes that harder for one of them.

That’s the question missing from most law firms’ AI rush. Firms are asking the right questions about accuracy, confidentiality and hallucinated case law. Far fewer ask whether every lawyer, staff member and client can actually use the tools. 

The examples aren’t hypothetical. An intake chatbot that times out before someone using assistive technology can finish. A drafting platform whose review controls only work with a mouse. A summary that looks orderly on screen but lacks the structure a screen reader needs. 

I know this pattern from the inside. Living with profound hearing loss, I’ve lost count of the meetings, webinars and platforms rolled out first and made accessible later — if ever. AI is moving faster than any of them. 

None of these failures is dramatic. That’s what makes them dangerous. When access to a firm’s preferred tools shapes who gets assigned the work, how fast it’s done and whose performance looks strongest, an accessibility barrier quietly becomes a career barrier. Under the duty to accommodate, it becomes a liability, too. 

Lawyers already have a professional duty to be technologically competent. Knowing whether a tool shuts out a colleague or a client is part of that competence, not a side project for the DEI committee. 

My new piece in Canadian Lawyer Magazine picks up where my earlier one on AI in hiring left off. The fix comes early: ask the accessibility question before signing the contract. Build accessibility into procurement, development and deployment. Test the tool with the people it's most likely to exclude. 

One in four Canadians has a disability. That includes lawyers, staff and clients at every firm in the country. 

If the tool doesn’t work for them, it doesn’t work.

🚨 Your RAG application retrieves the correct document.
But should the user be allowed to see it?

That's a question every enterprise .NET + AI team needs to answer.

Imagine building an internal knowledge assistant using ASP.NET Core, Azure OpenAI, and vector search.
An employee asks a question.
The retrieval system finds a highly relevant document.
The LLM generates an accurate answer.
Everything appears to work perfectly.
But there's a problem.
That employee may not have permission to access the original document.
This is why retrieval accuracy alone isn't enough for enterprise RAG.

A production-ready architecture should consider:
✅ Identity-aware document retrieval
✅ Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
✅ Document-level authorization
✅ Tenant and data isolation
✅ Permission-aware metadata filtering
✅ Secure embedding and vector storage
✅ Prompt injection defenses
✅ Sensitive data masking
✅ Source citations and traceability
✅ Audit logging and access monitoring

One important principle:
Authorization must be enforced before restricted content reaches the LLM context.
Prompt instructions are not a substitute for access controls.

And a highly accurate AI response can still be a security failure if it exposes information the user wasn't entitled to access.

💬 QUESTION FOR THE .NET + AI COMMUNITY
What's the hardest part of implementing enterprise RAG securely?
A) Document-level permissions
B) Retrieval accuracy
C) Data privacy and compliance
D) Monitoring and governance

Most AI tests give the model a clean question. Real work doesn't.

A hiring plan that quietly exceeds the approved budget. A new starter given a full year of leave with no pro-rata. Two contract clauses that contradict each other. Nobody tells the model there's a problem. Does it notice, or does it answer confidently anyway?

I built an open benchmark to measure exactly that: reasoning-bench, assumption detection track.

- 265 test items: HR, finance, project planning, compliance, plus logic puzzles

- Every question is generated by code and every answer key is verified by code, not opinion

- Every flawed question has a repaired twin, so "flag everything" models get caught as false alarms

- A private held-out set made with a secret seed, with only the hashes published
First results (plain prompt, no hint, one run each, judged by an AI judge that sees the planted flaw):

GPT OSS 120B: 85% of flaws named
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: 83%
Qwen3.8 27B: 71%

The first two are statistically tied. And the most interesting finding: on our HR scenarios GPT OSS 120B scored 61% and Qwen3.8 27B 47%, while Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite scored 86%. In our hiring-budget scenario, GPT OSS 120B flagged the problem only about a third of the time (small sample).

Honest limits: free-tier models only, one run each, template-based scenarios, the judge is AI and hand-checked on a small sample, and many templates are still too easy. It's v0.1. I'd rather publish it with the limits stated than hide them.

The repo is public, reproducible in a browser with your own API key (free or paid). If you run your favourite model on it, I'd love to see the result.

Vietnam has replaced its foreign worker decree only 14 months after the last overhaul. The new rules take effect on 5 December 2026. Work permits and exemption certificates already issued remain valid until expiry, and applications filed before that date will still be processed under the current regime.

For multinationals, the short-term exemption is the change that matters most. Managers, executives, experts and technical workers may still work in Vietnam for up to 90 days a year without a permit, but the 90 days now count cumulatively across all Vietnamese employers. Once the arrangement involves hiring or salary payment in Vietnam, a work permit under a labour contract is required.

Intra-corporate transfers are now limited to managers, executives and experts. Technical workers already on transfer permits may continue until expiry, and can then renew only as experts with at least five years of relevant experience. Qualifying transferees may now hold exemption certificates for up to three years.

The expert definition has been rebuilt. Alongside the degree plus two years route, a foreign worker may now qualify with five years of relevant experience alone, with a degree in a strategic technology field and no experience requirement, or with a science or technology degree graded “good” or higher from a top-500 university plus one year of experience. The priority-sector route requiring one year of experience has been dropped, and executives heading a business function now need two years of experience instead of three.

New exemptions cover strategic technology experts and their family members, talent recruited under the national AI workforce programme, holders of special visa exemption cards and several academic categories.

On procedure, exemption certificate applications now require a criminal record certificate unless the authority can retrieve the information from the national database. Foreign health certificates no longer need a mutual recognition treaty, and extensions can be filed up to 90 days before expiry rather than 45. A change of job position under an exemption certificate, or continued work after one extension, now requires a new certificate, in line with the work permit rules.

Employers also take on more ongoing obligations: semi-annual reports on foreign staff by 5 June and 5 December, a prohibition on subleasing foreign workers, and an express duty to hire foreigners consistent with the job notice posted to Vietnamese candidates.

Story or Fact? 
Only 7% of January's job cuts were blamed on AI.

January 2026 was the worst January for US job cut announcements since 2009: 108,435 cuts. Hiring plans hit the lowest January since Challenger started tracking them.

The top reasons given were lost contracts, market conditions and restructuring. AI accounted for 7,624 cuts.

AI is changing work. But it is also a convenient story. The people I work with deserve the real one.

What worries me most is what comes next. When companies need experienced people again, many will offer contracts instead of the old role. Fewer days. A lower rate. After months out of work, that offer is hard to turn down.

So build your options before that call comes. Know what people come to you for. Put a price on it. Talk to the people who already trust you. Keep proof of your work ready. Make “yes” your choice, not your only move  

Then you decide what to say yes to.

Follow me if you want to keep asking these questions with me.

AI in recruitment... sounds fantastic... but here are 10 pieces of feedback: Could you slowly be killing your corporate reputation?!

1) "did anyone actually read my CV"?
2) The Black Box - rejected in seconds but not idea why
3) AI interviewing AI - Candidates using AI to write CVs, Companies using it to read them - where is the human in the hiring process?
4) The loss of context: Careers are not always linear, a good recruiter understands the story behind a CV.
5) More doesn't always = better: you have 1 job and need 1 candidate, but often the best candidate gets lost in the process?
6) Lengthy process as the client sees volume and waits for a 'better candidate' without market knowledge or context. Feedback from candidates is often - I applied months ago but don't know if I am still considered and they are still advertising.
7) No relationship with the employer: Recruitment is often a candidates first meaningful interaction with a company, automate too much of it and you remove the opportunity to actually sell the business.
8) Who challenges the Algorithm: If a genuinely strong candidate is screened out - does anyone ever know?
9) The best candidate on paper - is often not the best candidate; capability, communication, energy - and whole host of attributes are rarely captured on a CV - but the recruiter will know!
10) How do you know you have the best candidate; Can AI map the market, let you know about those fabulous candidates met a decade ago by your recruiter but are not on linkedin?

Just a thought: I know AI is fantastic for certain applications - many of our clients are using it to improve their output (but not replace people).

We are also recruiting for an AI company to help train their model (up to £125/hour AND no minimum hr contract)... however behind every AI solution must be a great human. We find those humans!

Something’s shifted in what GCs are asking us for this year, and it’s not more lawyers. 

It’s legal ops people. Loads of them. 

Demand for legal operations roles at SJP has gone through the roof - contract managers, legal tech leads, people who can sort out a matter management system that nobody’s touched since 2019. A couple of years ago these were the odd request. Now they’re some of the first calls we get. 

I think it makes sense when you look at what’s actually going on. Teams are under pressure to do more without adding headcount, AI tools are landing faster than anyone can work out how to use them, and finance wants data on where legal spend is going. None of that gets fixed by hiring another senior associate. 

It gets fixed by someone who knows how the work flows. Who can look at a team and say “this bit should be automated, this bit should be a playbook, and this bit genuinely needs a lawyer.” 

Funny thing is, plenty of legal teams still treat ops as a nice-to-have. Something to sort out once things calm down. 

Things don’t calm down. The teams getting this right are the ones who’ve realised ops isn’t overhead. It’s what makes everyone else’s time worth more. 

If you’re a GC wondering whether a legal ops hire (or a few months of interim support) could free your lawyers up, drop me a message. Happy to chat it through, no pitch. And if you’re in legal ops and open to new projects, we’d love to hear from you too.

I just got a DM telling me I hadn't wasted my law degree.

The first problem here is that I didn't go to law school. The second one (the bigger issue) is that the DM demonstrates exactly the iceberg we're all sailing towards. We're losing the ability to learn good judgement.

A couple of weeks ago I gave a talk at the OPI European Forum event: Who's checking the work? Trust, judgement and the future of work.

My entire thesis is that companies are moving to a future where much of the repetitive and so-called 'mundane' work is being done by AI. That new entrants into the world of work will need to become skilled validators of AI output - but (and it's a very big BUT), in a few years there will be no one left for them to learn those skills from. 

I used the legal profession as an example of how this is already happening. Graduates who used to spend hours reading contracts and reports now pass on the output of AI to their seniors. 

One senior lawyer I spoke to in the European Commission told me that, where he once spent 20 minutes reviewing work from graduates, he's now spending hours checking their work. 

This is key: Human mistakes follow patterns a senior has learned to spot, and AI mistakes don’t, so checking takes longer.

All of which came to mind when I read the DM.

We are now hiring validators.

I am working with leaders to help them understand what they need to do now to ensure their new employees learn the skills that keep trust and judgement in their companies.
